commit.text:
The newspaper boy brought the threat folded inside an advertisement for winter coal. Elise found this almost considerate: the shop was cold, and an honest offer of fuel would have been more useful than another demand that Miriam surrender her licence. She spread the papers beneath the window, where the late light caught every uneven letter. The disputed leaflet accused the printer of issuing a notice under a name she had no right to use. It bore no signature of its own. The disputed leaflet carried a watermark shaped like a broken wheel. Elise held it above the clean sheet used to protect the composing stone. The wheel was pale and incomplete, as if somebody had lifted the paper before the mark was finished. A watermark could place a sheet in a history, though it could not tell her who had written the words upon it.

Jonas returned from the yard with rain on his cap. The workshop roll listed Jonas as Jonas Reed, apprentice. He had written the name himself, carefully, on the day Miriam took him on. Elise remembered because the capital R leaned in the opposite direction from the rest of his writing. Now he asked whether there was work he could finish out of sight of the front window. Miriam told him to dry his hands and bring the delivery book. Miriam entrusted the disputed leaflet to Jonas. He slipped it into his coat to keep it from the damp while lifting a stack of ledgers from the floor. Jonas believed the leaflet was still on Miriam’s desk, although he had folded it into his own coat. Elise saw him glance towards the empty desk, hesitate, and then lift the ledgers higher as though hard work might settle a question he had not spoken. She decided not to correct him in front of the newspaper boy.

The delivery cost three coins, a sum Elise had expected to spend on a proper meal after the late setting. The three-coin delivery left Elise with twenty-seven coins. “There are twenty-seven coins left,” Elise said. She counted the purse over the stone, grouping the remaining money into piles that would not roll beneath the cases. Jonas offered to postpone his wages until the matter was settled. Miriam answered too quickly that the matter would be settled in the morning. Elise disliked both offers. A threat had already begun to rearrange their lives before anyone had proved that it possessed authority. She paid the boy and made him sign for the amount, then asked where he had received the folded packet. At the corner, he said, from a man whose face he had not seen. It was the kind of answer that invited an attractive invention. She wrote only what he had actually said.

Pike arrived while she was warming a line of type beside the small stove. “The council has cancelled your licence,” Pike said. He did not show a council order. He said the official copy would follow and looked at the cold press as if it had already become somebody else's property. Elise asked which date the cancellation carried. The constable told her not to be clever. She had spent years being praised for clever fingers and punished for clever questions, and she kept her hand too close to the metal while deciding which reply would cost Miriam least. The hot type burned Elise’s right thumb. The pain was immediate and usefully simple. She put her thumb under the cold tap, asked again for the date, and watched Pike turn his attention to a crack in the floor. Miriam offered him a chair. He declined it as though sitting down might count as negotiation.

The press had been giving uneven impressions since its bed slipped during the summer move. Wet paper made the fault worse, dragging the weak side into a grey smear. Jonas brought a damp ream from the leaking corner before Elise could stop him. They tried one sheet, examined the blurred letters, and spread the rest too late to prevent staining. One ream was spoiled, leaving seven usable reams. She wrote the loss beside the delivery payment. The day now contained two kinds of subtraction, neither of which could be repaired by calling the threat a misunderstanding. Miriam suggested using the spoiled stock for wrappers when it dried. Elise agreed, but marked it unusable for printing. A wrapper was not a clean sheet merely because both began as paper. The distinction felt pedantic until she looked again at the accusation resting beneath the window.

After Pike left, Elise brought out a sample alphabet from each case they owned. One line of type contained a letter from a different font. The stray letter was wider than its neighbours, a small intrusion at the centre of an otherwise competent line. Jonas wanted to show it to the foreman at the mill at once. Elise said they should compare before they accused. Elise trusted Jonas with the leaflet but not yet with the account of how it had arrived. She asked him to retrieve the leaflet from his coat. His astonishment on finding it there was convincing enough to make her sorry for the suspicion, though not sorry enough to abandon the comparison. She set the samples beside the disputed line, leaving a finger's width between each so neither she nor Jonas could persuade a near match to become an exact one. Outside, the coal cart rattled past without stopping.

Miriam locked the wages drawer while the apprentices went home. Elise gave the typecase key to Miriam. Elise had no reason to keep the cases open after the day's work, and her burned thumb made the key difficult to turn. Elise knew Miriam held the typecase key. Miriam put it in the pocket she buttoned rather than the one with the loose seam. Miriam believed the county clerk would let them examine the register. She had known the clerk's mother and spoke as though a family acquaintance could still create a public right. Elise hoped she was correct, but planned to bring the shop's dated receipts as well. While Miriam searched for them, a packet slid out from beneath the ledger. Miriam kept a sealed packet addressed to a man called Dunn. She put it back so quickly that Jonas stopped sorting the samples. Nobody asked the obvious question. The silence gathered around the name and made it seem more dangerous than a spoken answer might have been.

Elise stayed beside the stone after Jonas went upstairs to fetch his coat. Elise remembered the attic room she had rented during her first apprenticeship. She had slept there above the cooper's hammering and carried her washing to a pump that froze every second winter. She could no longer put a year to the beginning of that apprenticeship. She remembered only the effort of learning to distinguish similar letters by touch when the candle failed. Tonight the same habit made her notice the wrong letter before she noticed the meaning of the sentence around it. It was a small competence and an inadequate defence against a constable, but it was hers. Elise could not decide whether the cart outside belonged to the constable. A cart stood beyond the window, its driver turned away under a broad hat. She could hear no conversation and would not claim that the shop was being watched merely because she was frightened enough to watch it herself.

Jonas came back with a clean rag for her thumb. He asked whether a man could lose the right to work because somebody had written an old name on an envelope. Elise said the answer ought to be no, then admitted that ought was a word people used when the record was incomplete. He folded the rag into a neat square and laid it on the stone. He had not answered a question she had not quite asked. Elise took the shop's licence copy from its frame, leaving a lighter rectangle on the wall. The paper carried a date, a fee, and a seal. None had changed since the morning. If the paper came from the county mill, its ledger might name the buyer. She planned to compare the watermarks after the morning delivery. The ledger, the register, and the type samples were three separate paths. She would not let the promise of one make her neglect the others.

Miriam sent Jonas to ask the neighbours for a dry place to store the unspoiled stock. Elise watched him cross the yard, then looked towards the bridge. Pike took his post at the stone toll bridge. Pike's coat made a dark patch beside the toll board. He had ordinary duties as well as the power to make an unsupported statement in their doorway, a fact she found harder to accommodate than an image of him as nothing but an enemy. She wrapped the burnt thumb, copied the licence date into her notebook, and prepared the samples for the morning. The printer's name at the foot of the disputed leaflet was wrong in a way that now seemed deliberate. She did not yet know whose purpose it served, and she resisted granting the mystery a single author before she had traced its paper.

Elise remained in the Holt print shop after the shutters were drawn. Miriam had gone to the back room, and the press stood beneath its canvas cover like a large animal that had finally stopped moving. Elise checked the drying stock once more and left enough space between the sheets for air. She was too tired to eat what remained of her bread. She dreamed that every letter in the shop had turned itself backwards. In the dream the reversed words were perfectly readable, but they accused her of something she could not remember doing. On waking in the chair beside the stone, she found the clean rag still wrapped around her thumb and the type still facing in its proper direction. Dawn had reached the window. The accusation had not become true while she slept, and neither had her hope that a record would be enough to defeat it. She opened the shutters and began packing the papers. Elise stayed inside the print shop while the delivery cart was loaded.

commit.text:
The county clerk objected to Elise's bundle before he looked at her licence. He said the counter was intended for documents, not an entire printing shop. She laid down the framed copy, the dated receipts, and a packet of sample letters, taking care to leave the wet umbrella on the floor. Elise reached the county records office before noon. The room smelled of polished wood and coal dust baked into cloth. A high clock worked through the silence with a faint scraping sound. She had expected an argument about authority. Instead she received a form asking which volume she wished to consult. She wrote the licence number, not the constable's accusation, and found that the smaller, answerable question made it possible to steady her hand.

Miriam arrived with the key and a basket of bread nobody had remembered to eat. Miriam returned the typecase key to Elise at the office door. Elise thanked her and checked the key's worn tooth against the indentation on her thumb bandage. The burn was healing beneath it, though turning a lock still hurt. A supplier intercepted them at the office door with money owed for an overcharged delivery. He apologised as if a minor mistake in his account might have caused the whole dispute. The supplier repaid five coins, bringing her purse to thirty-two. “The purse holds thirty-two coins,” Elise said. Elise signed the repayment line and kept it with the previous day's three-coin delivery receipt. Miriam said they could use the money to pay a solicitor. Elise said perhaps, after they knew which record needed defending. For once Miriam allowed a proposed expense to remain a proposal. They went back to the counter together.

Jonas stood under the clock, trying to make himself as narrow as the pillar beside it. Jonas waited in the county office while the register was copied. The clerk asked for his name to enter on the visitor sheet. He answered Reed, then stared at the old birth register the clerk had brought out with the mill papers. “Dunn was never my name,” Jonas said. His voice was loud enough to make two other visitors turn. Elise waited until the clerk had laid the volume flat. The birth register established that Jonas’s legal name was Jonas Dunn. The entry named his mother, her address at the time, and the occupation of a father who had worked for the mill. Jonas said Reed was the name by which he earned his wages. Elise answered that the register did not erase that life, but neither could a spoken denial erase the register. She asked permission to copy both names without deciding which one he ought to prefer.

He had brought the leaflet in an envelope folded inside his cap. Jonas passed the disputed leaflet to Elise. Elise placed it beside the retired watermark ledger, keeping the clerk's clean blotter between the two papers. The broken wheel appeared in the mill’s retired watermark ledger. The mill had stopped using that mark before Miriam's present licence began. It dated the stock, not yet the printing, but it narrowed the possible history. Jonas leaned closer, reading the old mill owner's name. Elise saw him recognise it and pull away. Elise suspected the packet linked Jonas to the mill’s former owner. That was an inference, not a relationship she could enter in the record on the strength of a glance. She asked him which line he knew. He said he would explain when Miriam returned from the bridge, and she disliked the bargain but accepted the wait. There were enough documents open on the table to require attention without forcing a confession beside them.

The licence register lay in a newer volume. The clerk turned to the proper page and ran a finger along the renewal entries. No cancellation followed the last fee. Elise knew the county register had not cancelled Miriam’s licence. Elise asked him to make a certified copy rather than merely tell her that Pike had been mistaken. He said the seal would take time, and she said she had brought bread. The clerk almost smiled. Miriam had been certain that acquaintance would open the volume; procedure had done it more plainly. Elise believed Miriam would return with a witness. Elise wrote a note asking for the public watch officer, folded it without sealing it, and sent the newspaper boy to find her. A witness would matter when the copied register had to be shown beyond this room. The boy left with two small loaves and strict instructions to repeat the written message rather than improve it.

While the seal was heated, Elise tried the sample letters against the disputed line again. The mismatched letter remained visible in the disputed line. Miriam had told her the letter must have come from their press because she recognised its slight tilt. The sample width made that impossible without a case none of them possessed. Miriam believed the mixed letter came from their press, but its width did not fit any case they owned. A familiar flaw could be copied or found in another workshop. Elise wrote the measurement beside her comparison and resisted the satisfaction of calling the matter solved. The accusation might be false even if the printer remained unknown. Her task was to establish the first proposition, not invent evidence for the second. Jonas held the ruler while she measured, and their hands stopped avoiding one another over the paper. Elise and Jonas agreed to compare the original records without concealing another name. He said the name on the packet was his father's. She thanked him for saying so without asking him to say more in the clerk's hearing.

Miriam returned without the watch officer. Mud covered the bottom of her skirt, and she had left the basket somewhere she could not remember. Miriam found Pike below the collapsed bridge arch; he was dead. A section of the bridge had fallen after the toll cart crossed. Miriam had gone down the bank with two workers and seen the body before the watch arrived. Elise pulled out a chair, then had to ask the clerk where the water was kept. The constable's threat had occupied the morning so completely that she struggled to make space for his death without turning it into another clue. His unsupported statement was still unsupported. His death required a separate record. She wrote the name of the worker who had stayed with Miriam, then stopped when Miriam asked her to wait. Some questions could be necessary without belonging to this exact minute.

The newspaper boy returned with the mill cart, which had taken the longer road after the bridge was closed. The driver had brought the replacement stock Miriam ordered before the dispute. Two dry reams arrived from the mill, increasing the usable stock to nine. Elise had him count the reams onto the dry office bench and sign the delivery book. The shop's seven usable reams remained there; the two newly delivered ones would join them when the cart reached the yard. She did not count the spoiled ream simply because it still occupied a shelf. Miriam watched the transaction and said Pike had promised to help carry the paper if the road flooded. It was a memory Elise had no place for in the argument she had been preparing against him. She accepted it as something Miriam had heard and left the silence that followed unfilled.

The clerk found an old correction proof in the packet of related shop filings. A correction proof bore the same date as the unopened packet. Miriam looked at the date and closed her eyes. The sealed packet itself was still at the shop, but Elise had copied its postmark into her notebook before leaving. The dates matched. A coincidence was possible; a connection would need the contents. If the broken wheel belonged to an older mill mark, the leaflet might predate the accusation. She set the thought aside beside the mill mark. She intended to print a correction once the paper had dried. She would not use the damaged press on wet stock to make an urgent correction look clean. They could wait for the paper, open the packet with Jonas present, and prepare a statement that distinguished what the documents established from what the people remembered. Miriam asked whether the statement would say anything about the dead constable. Elise said it would report his unsupported claim without assigning him a motive.

As the clerk tied the certified copy with green tape, Elise rested her burning thumb on the edge of the table. Elise recalled closing the print-shop shutters on the first evening of the dispute. That had been the first evening, before the county visit, with the lamp reflected in the disputed watermark and Pike still at his bridge post. She could locate the remembered action without making it her current location. Now the clock above Jonas was approaching noon, and the clerk was pressing a seal into wax. The sequence mattered because fear had already begun rearranging it in her mind, pushing the collapse backwards until it seemed to shadow every word Pike had spoken. Elise listed the events in order. The list could not tell her how to feel about him, but it prevented those feelings from changing when he had died.

She dozed on the office bench while they waited for the last signature. She dreamed Pike stood at the bridge collecting coins from the rain. He held a ledger that never became wet, and each coin made the same sound as the county clock. Waking, she found Jonas watching the door and Miriam repairing a torn hem with a pin. The register copy was ready. Elise placed it inside the frame that had held the shop licence, protecting the seal with a fold of clean paper. They would take the road through the square because the bridge was closed now in fact, whatever claims had circulated before. She asked Jonas to carry the sample type and left the disputed leaflet inside her own document case. The clerk wrote their departure in the visitor book under both of Jonas's names. Elise waited inside the county records office while their return carriage was called.

details.text:
I stand with ink close enough to stain my sleeve. I want a line that can be read without asking a frightened person to supply what it leaves out. The clean sheet came off the press so quietly that Elise thought for a moment the type had failed to touch it. She lifted the corner and saw the heading hold its edge against the pale paper. They had waited for the stock to dry, tightened the damaged bed, and rejected two trial sheets before attempting the public copy. There was no miracle in the impression, only the accumulation of small refusals to hurry. Elise carried the first clean correction to the market square. The square was filling with carts diverted from the broken bridge. A notice about the collapse hung beside a notice about the price of flour. Elise waited for a space on the public board large enough to hold the correction without covering either. Truth did not become more public by making another useful fact disappear.

The council had heard the evidence that morning. Miriam retained her existing rights, and Elise had applied under her own name after the clerk pointed out that years of work did not automatically enter a printer on the register. The council register entered Elise as a licensed master printer. She had expected triumph and felt instead the weight of the title, a responsibility too late to protect them from yesterday's rumour and early enough to govern what she printed tomorrow. The clerk gave her a numbered copy. She read the number back before signing. She paid four coins for the public notice and had twenty-eight left. “Twenty-eight coins remain,” Elise said. The payment left a smaller purse and a document she could show anyone who asked which authority permitted her work. A man waiting behind her muttered that a printed correction was merely another printed claim. She agreed and showed him the register reference at its foot.

Jonas came from the shop carrying the shop's retained proofs in a dry envelope. Elise placed the typecase key in Jonas’s hand. Elise asked him to put the dated copies in the locked case when he returned. He said he would keep the disputed names visible in the index, not file the matter under a comforting general heading. Elise trusted Jonas to keep the proofs without hiding inconvenient names. She had no promise that he would never conceal another painful detail. Trust meant allowing him a duty whose performance she could see. Jonas believed the apprentices would keep their own dated copies. He had begun to speak of the younger boys as apprentices rather than rivals, which made the new responsibility sound less like a favour she had done him. Jonas returned to the Holt print shop to unlock the cases. Elise watched him turn towards the side street, his shoulders held at a different angle from the previous morning. She could not tell whether relief or fear was moving him faster, and decided she did not need to know before letting him go.

I keep the shape of the letter in my mind. I can hear the street beyond the window while I wait for the paper to tell me less than a rumour promises. Miriam brought the sealed packet at last, opened in Jonas's presence before they left the shop. “I kept the packet because I was afraid of losing him,” Miriam said. The admission had cost her more than she had expected. She had hoped to defend her silence as loyalty and discovered that the same word had served Jonas as an excuse to deny his name. The packet contained Jonas’s mother’s apprenticeship request under the name Dunn. His mother had asked the printer to take him in under a name that would spare him the mill owner's enmity. Jonas had believed the packet was an accusation, but it contained his mother’s request for an apprenticeship. The request was a record of somebody trying to provide a future, not a proof that every choice made to protect him had been right. Miriam allowed Elise to copy the relevant passage while keeping the original in its envelope. They agreed the public correction needed the printing evidence; Jonas's family history belonged in it only where he chose to make it relevant.

The workers' secretary arrived with a folder and two witnesses. The workers’ society accepted the disputed leaflet as evidence. The original would remain available for comparison rather than disappear into a stove once it had become inconvenient. Elise showed the witnesses the watermark under the light and then showed them the dated ledger copy. The retired watermark and dated ledger identified the paper stock as older than the licence period named in the accusation. The stock had been made before the licence period named in the accusation. That fact did not alone identify every person who later handled a sheet, so the correction did not pretend otherwise. Elise knew the accusation had relied on paper older than Miriam’s licence. The accusation’s printing date remained unproved by the watermark alone. She printed the dates side by side, trusting readers with the comparison instead of demanding belief in her character. The secretary signed for the leaflet and wrote where anyone could inspect it during the society's open hours.

The wrong letter had led them to a private case kept by the former mill owner. His estate inventory listed the wider sorts, and the county sample carried the same chipped edge. The mismatched letter belonged to the former mill owner’s private press. Miriam had recognised the tilt because she had seen the owner's notices years before, not because the letter had lived in their own shop. Elise explained this without making recognition itself a fault. The mistake lay in allowing recognition to become certainty without a measurement. The mixed font did not prove who had set the disputed line on a particular day. It did establish that the shop's own cases were not its only possible source. She chose a restrained sentence for the correction and rejected the secretary's suggestion that a stronger adjective would make people read it. A stronger adjective would not make the case fit their measurements more closely.

The dated proof settled a smaller, more personal doubt. The dated proof showed Miriam had prepared a correction before the threat arrived. Miriam had prepared it and then hidden it with the packet because she feared that publishing the names would drive Jonas away. She had not invented the correction after Pike's arrival. Elise asked why she had been willing to let the shop suffer rather than show it. Miriam said she had mistaken waiting for kindness. There was no useful reply that would repair the lost day, so Elise helped her put the documents in the order in which they had been made. Miriam stood beside Elise in the market square. People who had ignored the printer that morning now stopped to ask her what the seal meant. She answered the question patiently, sometimes handing them the frame so they could examine it without leaning over Elise's bandaged hand.

I watch the edge of the sheet lift in the light. I am trying to keep a measured width separate from the name somebody wants me to accuse. The correction consumed more stock than the urgent first notice had. They needed copies for the board, the council, the workers' room, and customers who would otherwise hear only the first rumour. The correction used three reams, leaving six. Elise wrote the final count in the delivery book and made clear which three reams had become finished copies. The seven from the first evening had gained two dry replacements before losing these three; the spoiled ream never re-entered the usable total. She thought of the cold attic where a travelling compositor had once shown her how to listen before striking a loose letter into place. Elise remembered an itinerant compositor teaching her to listen for a loose sort, at a time she could not date. She could remember the sound of his teaching better than the year or even the spelling of his name. Not every useful past fact came with a convenient date, and she left the date blank rather than supplying one that felt plausible.

At the edge of the gathering, a man in a dark hat stood without taking a sheet. Elise could not know whether the silent man at the edge of the crowd had read the notice. He might have been unable to read, unwilling to carry evidence, or simply waiting for someone who had gone to buy flour. Elise disliked how readily fear made the first two possibilities into accusations. She asked the newspaper boy to leave extra copies at the counter instead of following the man. If the public kept the correction, the false leaflet might lose its authority. A correction could be kept, ignored, argued over, or wrapped around a parcel. Printing it made those futures possible without deciding which would occur. She intended to teach the apprentices to keep every dated proof. She would teach the apprentices to preserve dated proofs because records had helped them, not because records made every reader fair. The boy folded a copy into his pocket, this time with the heading facing inward to protect it from the rain.

I feel the roughness of the proof under my hand. I am here with the work unfinished, and the next impression has not yet been made. Miriam asked whether the shop window should be repainted to include Elise's new title. Elise said they could discuss it after the accounts were copied. There had been enough permanent decisions made under pressure. They returned to the narrow street, where Jonas had opened the cases and laid the proof envelope on the dry stone. He showed them the index before asking about supper. Nothing had been filed under scandal or vindication. There were dates, names, document numbers, and a short note directing the reader from Reed to Dunn. Elise touched the edge of the page with her unburned hand. The ordinary usefulness of that note seemed more durable than the praise she had received at the square. She asked him to make a second copy for the workers' room and went to light the small stove.

The shop quieted before dark. Elise put the press under its canvas and checked that the remaining six reams were raised above the damp floor. She dreamed of a press making no sound at all. In sleep she stood beside it waiting for an impression that would never arrive, unable to decide whether the silence meant peace or failure. She woke to the sound of Jonas closing a case correctly, without dropping its lid. The street outside had grown dark, and the corrected notice would still be there when morning readers came. Its paper could become wet and its edges could tear. For tonight the shop held a clean proof, a dated register copy, and a key in the custody they had recorded. Elise listened to the ordinary rattle of type being put away and allowed the unfinished work to remain unfinished until morning. Elise returned to the market square to collect the frame from the notice board. Pike walked into the present scene alive and uninjured and asked a question.
